summary: Defines terminology and requirements for sending a location URI that points to a person's location, instead of putting the location itself in a message. It is requirements work for Internet signaling and messaging. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Location-by-Reference shares a URI that points to location information, rather than placing the location object directly in a message. RFC 5808 lists requirements for creating that URI and for retrieving the location while protecting privacy.

questions: location by reference vs location by value
how should a location uri be constructed
subtitle: Requirements for sharing a location URI instead of location data in a message.

tldr.problem: Sending a location object directly in every message may not fit an application's privacy, power, or information-sharing needs.
tldr.mechanism: Location-by-Reference uses a location URI that a recipient can resolve. RFC 5808 sets requirements for protocols that create and cancel the URI and for protocols that retrieve the location.
tldr.outcome: The Informational RFC defines terminology and requirements, not a complete protocol. It calls for controls such as expiry, cancellation, authentication, confidentiality, and difficult-to-guess references by default.

today: RFC 5808 is Informational and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Location by Value and by Reference
sections.content:
With Location-by-Value, a message carries the location object itself, such as a PIDF-LO. With Location-by-Reference, the message carries a URI that a recipient later uses to obtain location information. RFC 5808 covers the reference approach and leaves Location-by-Value out of scope.

The RFC identifies cases where a reference may help: a mobile device may avoid repeatedly querying a location server, a third party may retrieve and publish the location, or an operator may want to limit how widely location information is available. A URI refers to the target's current location, though the returned value may remain unchanged for a time.
sections.plainLanguage: One method sends the location itself; the other sends a URI that can be used to retrieve it. The URI approach can separate sharing a reference from retrieving the location.

sections.title: The URI Life Cycle and Participants
sections.content:
The location URI life cycle has five stages: creation, distribution, conveyance, dereference, and termination. A Location Configuration Protocol handles creation, distribution, and termination; a Location Dereference Protocol retrieves the location. Conveyance of the URI between signaling participants is outside this document's scope.

The target obtains a URI from a location server and passes it to a location recipient. The recipient dereferences it at the server, which applies the Rule Maker's policy. The configuration and dereference stages do not have to use the same protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A target obtains a reference, shares it with a recipient, and the recipient asks a location server to resolve it. The server applies the location policy before returning information.

sections.title: Expiry, Authorization and URI Construction
sections.content:
A location URI may expire or be cancelled. Expiry lets a server track whether a reference remains valid, limits how long a leaked URI can be used, and may prevent a recipient from tracking a target indefinitely.

The access-control model makes the server decide who may dereference a URI, and the URI must not itself contain location information. Under the possession model, possession of the URI grants access, so the URI is confidential and needs enough randomness to resist guessing. By default, it must not identify the target.
sections.plainLanguage: A reference can stop working after its lifetime or after cancellation. If possession of the URI grants access, anyone who obtains it may be able to retrieve the location.

sections.title: Requirements for Configuration and Retrieval
sections.content:
The configuration protocol must support a location URI, indicate its lifetime when limited, and support cancellation. By default, URIs must be random and unique for their lifetime, must not reveal location-specific components, and must not identify the target. A URI with 128 bits of randomness is recommended.

The dereference protocol must support URI references, mechanisms to authenticate client and server, and return a well-formed PIDF-LO. It must support resolving the same URI more than once according to server configuration and protect the confidentiality of messages between recipient and server.
sections.plainLanguage: The reference should be hard to guess, avoid identifying the target, and have a stated lifetime when it expires. The retrieval protocol must authenticate its parties and protect the returned location.
